item.research_question: What is the specific atomic structure of lithium-intercalated MoS2 monolayers, and how does this structure determine the catalytic activation of the normally inert basal plane for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER)?
item.material_system: Molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) and Tungsten disulfide (WS2) monolayers; specifically the 2H (trigonal prismatic), 1T (octahedral), 1T′ (clustered Mo), and 1T′′ (zig-zag chain) polymorphs.
item.processing_route: Lithium intercalation by immersing MoS2 powder in 1 M n-butyl lithium for 72 to 240 hours at room temperature, followed by transfer to water, sonication for exfoliation, and purification via centrifugation and dialysis.
item.test_conditions: Photocatalytic HER in basic solution (pH 11) using Eosin Y as a sensitizer and Triethanolamine (TEOA) as a sacrificial electron donor, irradiated with a xenon lamp at 1 sun; structural analysis via aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) at 200 kV.
key_findings: Lithium intercalation directs a preferential transformation of the basal plane from 2H to the 1T′ phase, which becomes the energetically preferred metastable state.
The Gibbs free energy of hydrogen adsorption (ΔGH) for the 2H basal plane is +1.6 eV, rendering it catalytically inert.
The 1T′ transformation lowers ΔGH to +0.18 eV (specifically 0.13 eV at 1/16 coverage), making the basal plane amenable to hydrogen adsorption.
Fully transformed 1T′ MoS2 yields a peak H2 flux of 620 nmol min−1, which is four times higher than the autocatalytic EY dye control (150 nmol min−1).
H2 yield scales proportionately with the fraction of 1T′ transformation present in the sample.
When hydrogen coverage exceeds 0.4, the 1T′ phase becomes more stable than the 2H phase.
The ΔGH of 1T′ MoS2 is comparable to 2H MoS2 edges on Au(111), one of the most active HER catalysts known.
WS2 undergoes analogous phase transformation but shows a 10-fold reduction in ΔGH compared to 2H WS2, resulting in lower HER efficiency than MoS2.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that lithium intercalation induces a structural distortion where Mo atoms cluster asymmetrically to form the 1T′ phase. This specific atomic arrangement alters the electronic energetics, lowering the hydrogen binding energy (ΔGH) from a strongly unfavorable +1.6 eV to a near-optimal +0.18 eV. This thermodynamic shift allows the basal plane to actively adsorb hydrogen and facilitate the HER, a function previously limited only to edge sites in the 2H phase. The catalytic enhancement is further driven by the 1,000-fold increase in surface area availability upon exfoliation to monolayers.
item.limitations: The text notes that previous structural interpretations were confused by incomplete transformations, partial intercalation, and the reversion of the metastable 1T′ phase back to 2H during characterization (e.g., under electron beam illumination or heating).
item.future_work: The authors propose that establishing these structure-property relationships provides a pathway towards the quantitative engineering of MX2 materials to enable the emerging 'green energy' economy.
quotes: lithium intercalation to direct a preferential transformation of the basal plane from 2H (trigonal prismatic) to 1T′ (clustered Mo).
the 1T′ transformation renders the normally inert basal plane amenable towards hydrogen adsorption and hydrogen evolution.
lowering of ΔGH from +1.6 eV for 2H to +0.18 eV for 1T′, comparable to 2H molybdenum disulfide edges on Au(111)
